title: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state: the first hours

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the ADA consensus on hyperglycaemic crises. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.why: Glucose is usually over 250 but can be near normal, especially on an SGLT-2 inhibitor. The distractors describe the hyperosmolar state.

questions.q: Above what serum osmolality is the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state diagnosed?
questions.why: With glucose over 600, minimal ketosis, and often altered mental status. Fluid deficits are larger than in ketoacidosis, and the patients are older and sicker.

questions.q: What is the first treatment in diabetic ketoacidosis, before insulin?
questions.a: Intravenous isotonic fluid, about a litre in the first hour
questions.why: Fluids alone lower glucose and restore perfusion. Insulin started before the potassium is known can drop it to a dangerous level.

questions.q: Below what potassium is insulin withheld until potassium has been replaced?
questions.why: Total body potassium is low even when the serum value is high, and insulin drives it into cells. Between 3.3 and 5.2, potassium is added to every litre of fluid.

questions.q: What is the standard insulin infusion rate in diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.why: With or without a 0.1 unit per kg bolus. The glucose should fall by 50 to 75 mg/dL an hour; if it does not, the rate is doubled.

questions.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, at what glucose is dextrose added to the fluids?
questions.why: The insulin continues, at a lower rate, because it is treating the ketosis, not the glucose. In the hyperosmolar state the switch point is 300.

questions.q: Which findings mark resolution of diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.why: Two of the three, with glucose under 200. Urine ketones lag behind because the strip measures acetoacetate, which rises as beta-hydroxybutyrate is cleared.

questions.q: How long before stopping the insulin infusion should the first subcutaneous basal insulin be given?
questions.why: Intravenous insulin lasts minutes. Without overlap the ketoacidosis returns within hours, which is the commonest cause of a second infusion.

questions.q: Below what pH is sodium bicarbonate considered in diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.why: Above that it does not improve outcomes and may worsen hypokalemia and cerebral oedema. Insulin and fluids correct the acidosis on their own.

questions.q: Which are common precipitants of diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.why: New-onset type 1 diabetes is the other. The search for a precipitant runs alongside treatment; an ECG and cultures are routine.

questions.q: A patient on empagliflozin has abdominal pain, vomiting, ketones and a pH of 7.2 with a glucose of 180 mg/dL. What is this?
questions.why: The near-normal glucose delays the diagnosis. Treatment is the same as ordinary ketoacidosis, with dextrose added from the start because the glucose is already low.

questions.q: How often are electrolytes checked during treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.why: Glucose is checked hourly. The anion gap, not the glucose, tells you whether the ketoacidosis is resolving.
